feedbackForCompany.finalReport:
During my internship at Envision Wind Power Station in Navoi Region, I gained valuable practical knowledge about wind energy, workplace safety, and the operation of large-scale renewable energy facilities. The internship combined theoretical lectures, practical exercises, and field visits that helped me better understand the wind power industry.
On the first day, after arriving at the wind power station operated by ACWA Power and Envision, we attended a safety briefing focused on local wildlife hazards. We learned how to identify venomous and non-venomous snakes, studied different types of venom and their symptoms, and received instructions on how to respond if dangerous animals were encountered. We also visited areas where these animals are commonly found to better understand the environmental conditions around the station.
During the second day, we visited several wind turbines located in the surrounding steppe. This field trip allowed us to observe the turbines in operation and learn about the environment in which they are installed. Later, we attended a lecture explaining the structure of wind turbines, the materials used in their construction, and the principles of converting wind energy into electrical energy. As part of a practical activity, we built small wind turbine rotors to better understand aerodynamic principles.
The third day focused on the construction and installation of wind turbines. We learned about the manufacturing process of turbine components, soil preparation, and foundation construction. We also studied the internal structure of wind turbines and learned why modern turbines typically use three blades. In the afternoon, we received training on Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) and participated in practical exercises, including climbing to a height of five meters while following proper safety procedures under professional supervision.
The fourth day was dedicated to advanced safety training. We learned about different types of PPE, equipment inspection, safety regulations, and workplace incident statistics. We also studied emergency procedures, including evacuation methods during a fire and rescue techniques for assisting workers who become unconscious inside a turbine.
On the final day, we visited Ayakagytma Lake near the wind farm and learned about the local geography and environmental characteristics of the region. This visit helped us better understand the natural conditions surrounding renewable energy projects.
Overall, this internship provided valuable insight into wind power generation, engineering safety practices, and renewable energy technologies. The experience strengthened my interest in electrical power engineering and helped me connect academic knowledge with real industrial applications.

feedbackForCompany.finalReport:
Day 1 - June 2, 2026

On June 2, 2026, we arrived at the Wind Power Plant (WPP) located in the Navoi Region. The power plant is operated by ACWA Power and Envision. After arriving, we settled into our accommodation and went to the canteen at 12:00 PM for lunch. After lunch, we were given free time to rest until 2:00 PM.

At 2:00 PM, we were taken to the main office building, where we attended a safety briefing. During the briefing, we learned how to behave when encountering wild animals and what actions to take in the event of an animal attack. We also learned how to distinguish venomous snakes from non-venomous ones, studied different types of venom and their symptoms, and visited the natural habitats of local wildlife.

At 6:00 PM, we returned to the canteen for dinner. After dinner, everyone went back to their rooms to rest.

Day 2 – June 3, 2026

At 8:00 AM, we gathered and went to the canteen for breakfast. We were then asked to assemble at 9:30 AM for a field trip to observe the surrounding environment and visit the wind turbines.

We successfully reached the wind turbines and took a walk through the steppe surrounding the site. At 11:30 AM, we returned to the accommodation. After lunch, we waited until 2:00 PM for the day's lecture.

The lecture focused on wind turbines, including their components and operating principles. At the end of the session, we built small model wind turbine rotors with our own hands. After the lecture, we returned to the canteen, had dinner, and then went back to our rooms to rest.

Day 3 – June 4, 2026

At 9:00 AM, we gathered in the main office building for another lecture that continued the topic of wind turbines.

During this session, we learned how the various components of a wind turbine are manufactured and how the soil and foundations are prepared before installation. We also studied the internal structure of a wind turbine, the functions of its components, and the reason why modern wind turbines typically have three blades.

After lunch, at 2:00 PM, we returned to the main building for training on Personal Protective Equipment (PPE). Following the theoretical session, we moved to a specially prepared training area where we put on the required safety equipment and completed a supervised climb to a height of five meters. Under the guidance of experienced professionals, we successfully followed all safety procedures.

Day 4 – June 5, 2026

At 9:00 AM, we gathered in the main building and continued our PPE training. We learned about different types of protective equipment, proper safety procedures, the service life of safety gear, and their specific purposes.

We also studied statistics on the most common workplace incidents and their associated fatality risks.

After lunch, at 2:00 PM, we continued the PPE training. We learned how to respond during emergency situations, including how to evacuate a wind turbine in the event of a fire and how to rescue a worker who has lost consciousness inside the turbine. After the training session, we returned to the accommodation and rested.

Day 5 – June 6, 2026

At 8:30 AM, we were asked to gather for an excursion. We boarded vehicles and traveled to Lake Ayakagitma, located not far from the power plant. The journey took approximately 30 to 45 minutes.

Upon arrival, we were given information about the lake, including the reasons why the soil in the area is soft and why salt patterns can be observed on the sand. We learned about the local geography and environmental characteristics of the region.

After our visit and the registration of our arrival, we returned to the power plant. Before departure, we had been instructed to clean our rooms and pack our belongings to ensure that we would be ready on time.

After arriving back at the accommodation, we packed our belongings and officially departed from the wind power plant, marking the end of our educational visit.
feedbackForCompany.finalComments: The five days we spent at the wind power station were both informative and enjoyable. We highly appreciated the instructors, lectures, practical training sessions, and the living conditions provided during our stay. The entire program was organized professionally, and all aspects were maintained at a very high standard.

During my five-day internship at a chemical-spectral laboratory, I had the opportunity to observe various analytical methods and laboratory procedures used in chemical analysis. The main purpose of the internship was to gain an understanding of laboratory operations and modern analytical techniques.

Throughout the internship, I observed the work of laboratory specialists and learned about several analytical methods. One of the topics covered was oxidation-reduction analytical methods, where I learned about the principles used to determine the chemical composition of different samples. I also observed the spectrometry process and gained a better understanding of how instruments are used to identify and measure elements and compounds.

In addition, I was introduced to the Grand-Potok analysis system and atomic emission analysis. The laboratory staff explained the operating principles of the equipment, the stages of sample preparation, and the importance of accuracy and quality control in analytical work. Through these observations, I became familiar with the workflow of a professional laboratory environment and the responsibilities of laboratory personnel.

Due to safety regulations and the nature of the equipment, interns were not allowed to directly operate the instruments or perform laboratory procedures independently. Instead, our role was to carefully observe the processes, take notes, and ask questions to better understand the methods being demonstrated. This approach allowed us to focus on learning the theoretical and practical aspects of laboratory analysis while maintaining a safe working environment.

At the end of the internship, we completed a test based on the materials and analytical methods that had been presented during the training period. This helped evaluate our understanding of the topics covered throughout the internship.

Overall, the internship was a valuable educational experience that improved my knowledge of chemical analysis, laboratory organization, and modern analytical technologies. It provided useful insight into professional laboratory work and helped connect the theoretical knowledge gained at university with real industrial practices.

feedbackForCompany.finalReport:
During my five-day placement at the chemical-spectral laboratory, I had the privilege of observing a wide range of advanced analytical methodologies and standard operating procedures critical to modern chemical analysis. The primary objective of this internship was to gain comprehensive insight into professional laboratory workflows, quality control systems, and cutting-edge analytical instrumentation.
​Over the course of the week, I closely monitored the daily routines of senior laboratory technicians and deepened my understanding of several core diagnostic techniques. One of the key areas examined was reduction-oxidation (redox) analytical methods, where I learned how these chemical concepts are practically applied to determine the elemental composition of various samples. Additionally, observing the spectrometry division provided valuable clarity on how automated instruments are calibrated to detect, isolate, and quantify specific chemical structures and elements.
​Furthermore, I was introduced to the operational mechanics of the "Grand-Potok" automated analysis system alongside atomic emission spectrometry. The laboratory personnel explained the technical design of these units, the precise steps required for sample preparation, and why rigorous quality assurance is vital to prevent errors in the final data. These demonstrations offered a realistic perspective on how a high-throughput laboratory functions and the level of accountability expected from engineering professionals.
​To comply with strict institutional safety policies and protect sensitive equipment, interns did not engage in direct manual operation of the machinery. Instead, our responsibilities focused on systematic observation, meticulous note-taking, and active technical dialogue with the staff. This pedagogical approach allowed us to thoroughly absorb both the theoretical foundations and practical nuances of industrial analysis while maintaining an incident-free workspace.
​At the conclusion of the program, our progress was evaluated through a comprehensive examination covering all the analytical methods and materials introduced during the training sessions. This assessment served as a valuable metric to verify our understanding of the techniques reviewed.
​In summary, this internship proved to be an invaluable academic asset that expanded my proficiency in chemical analysis, laboratory management, and industrial technology. It successfully bridged the gap between the abstract concepts taught in university lectures and the fast-paced realities of contemporary industrial chemistry.
feedbackForCompany.finalComments: This internship was an exceptional learning experience that seamlessly connected my university studies with real-world laboratory practices. Observing advanced analytical techniques and professional workflows firsthand has greatly enhanced my understanding of chemical engineering and laboratory operations. I am very grateful for the guidance provided by the laboratory staff and the university throughout this program."

feedbackForCompany.finalReport:
During my internship as a Thermal Power and Wind Engineering Intern at Envision Energy, I had the invaluable opportunity to bridge my academic foundation from Samarkand International University of Technology (SIUT) with the cutting-edge realities of the renewable energy sector. Over the course of the internship, my primary focus was exploring how modern wind power technologies integrate with traditional energy grids, using data-driven methods to analyze turbine efficiency.
One of my core responsibilities involved using Envision’s specialized digital environment to track and monitor real-time SCADA telemetry data from operational smart wind turbines. I analyzed key parameters such as rotor speeds, generator temperatures, and pitch configurations to evaluate aerodynamic efficiency. Under the close supervision of my mentor, I participated in compiling a comprehensive technical report that examined localized power curve deviations. By cross-referencing real-time sensor metrics with theoretical fluid dynamics formulas, our team identified minor pitch misalignments on two active turbines. Correcting these issues demonstrated a potential 2% optimization in localized annual energy production (AEP), showcasing the vital role of predictive maintenance.
Beyond the technical tasks, this experience significantly accelerated my professional growth. Navigating massive industrial datasets and adapting to a fast-paced, safety-first corporate environment initially posed a challenge. However, through the exceptional mentorship provided by Envision’s engineering team and the communication skills fostered by SIUT, I successfully overcame these hurdles. I learned to interpret complex engineering blueprints, Piping and Instrumentation Diagrams (P&IDs), and automated control sequences.
In conclusion, this internship has deeply influenced my career trajectory. It has shifted my professional focus entirely toward smart grids and sustainable energy systems optimization. The combination of supportive mentorship, an innovative work culture, and rigorous academic preparation made this experience highly rewarding. I am incredibly grateful to both Envision and SIUT for collaborating to provide such a seamless, impactful, and technically enriching internship program.
feedbackForCompany.finalComments: This internship was a transformative experience that solidified my engineering aspirations. I want to express my deepest gratitude to my mentor at Envision and the faculty at SIUT for making this opportunity possible.

Internship Report

During my internship period, I gained valuable knowledge and practical understanding of the oil and gas industry through a combination of classroom training, field demonstrations, and assessments.

On the first day of the internship, we attended a comprehensive safety training session that lasted approximately three to four hours. During this session, company specialists explained the importance of workplace safety, emergency procedures, personal protective equipment (PPE), and the rules that must be followed while working in industrial environments. This training helped us understand how to maintain a safe working environment and prevent accidents.

Throughout the internship, our daily schedule included a one-hour lunch break at 12:00 PM. On the second day, we participated in additional classroom lessons focused on the oil extraction process. The instructors explained how oil is discovered, drilled, extracted, processed, and transported. We learned about different stages of production and the technologies used in the industry.

Later that day, we attended a practical training session at the company’s training polygon. There, an experienced professional gave a detailed presentation using geological cross-sections and profile views of the Earth. The presentation illustrated underground formations, drilling operations, well structures, and pipeline systems. This session helped us better understand the relationship between geological conditions and oil production activities.

On the fourth day, we spent the entire training period at the polygon, where we learned about various oil extraction machines and equipment. The instructors demonstrated how the machinery operates and explained its role in the production process. We also learned about the responsibilities of workers in different positions, including equipment operators, technicians, and field personnel. This practical training provided valuable insight into the daily operations of an oil production facility.

During the internship at Envision, the primary focus was on foundational training in wind energy safety and basic turbine knowledge. The program was designed to prepare interns for safe operations in wind turbine environments through structured theoretical and practical training.

A major part of the internship involved attending safety classes aligned with Global Wind Organisation Basic Safety Training (GWO-BST) standards. These sessions covered essential safety modules including working at heights, fire awareness, first aid, and manual handling. Successful completion of this training resulted in obtaining a GWO-BST certificate, which is internationally recognized in the wind energy industry.

Practical safety training was conducted at the base of the wind turbine tower. This included the correct use of fall protection equipment such as rope grabs and double lanyards. Exercises focused on safe climbing procedures and proper use of personal protective equipment in high-risk environments.

In addition, emergency response simulations were performed to develop practical safety skills. These included rescuing an unconscious person suspended on a rope system, applying first aid techniques on a mannequin, using a fire extinguisher to control simulated fires, and applying bandages to treat wounds. These exercises provided hands-on experience in handling emergency situations in a controlled environment.

Theoretical classes on wind turbine working principles were also conducted. These lessons introduced the basic structure and operation of wind turbines, including key components such as the nacelle, hub, blades, and tower, as well as the general process of energy conversion.

Up to this stage, all training activities have been carried out in classroom and at the base of the turbine tower. No direct maintenance or component-level field operations have been performed yet, as the focus has been on safety preparation and fundamental understanding.

Overall, the internship provided essential training in safety procedures, emergency response, and basic turbine structure, forming a strong foundation for future technical work in wind turbine maintenance and operation.

While the role required developing a sharp attention to detail to handle complex multi-layered trade regulations, it also highlighted key systemic friction points. Early operational coordination gaps and localized logistical constraints slowed down initial workflows. In conclusion, this internship provided invaluable practical exposure to localized international trade execution and digital customs automation. Successfully executing these digital workflows has solidified my career aspirations to specialize in supply chain digitalization and the optimization of digital trade corridors across Central Asia.

During my internship at the factory, I was introduced to the 1C software system and learned how employees’ salaries are calculated. Salary calculations are based on timesheets submitted by the Human Resources Department to the Accounting Department. I also studied the Payroll Register (Form T-51), which contains employee information such as full name, personal income tax data, pension fund contributions, sick leave payments, employer-paid leave, compensation payments, benefits, meal allowances, and termination records. This form includes all personal and payroll-related information of employees.
In addition, I became familiar with the process of checking salary payments for the previous month using a computer system. I learned that if an employee receives less than the amount due, the remaining balance is carried forward and added to the employee’s salary in the following month.
I also met with the factory economist and learned about planning and economic activities within the organization. The economist explained the importance of budgeting in any enterprise, including income and expense budgeting, procurement budgeting, and payment planning. It is necessary to regularly monitor and compare financial indicators with previous periods to ensure effective financial management and informed decision-making within the organization.

During the internship, an intensive professional qualification program for the "Oil and Gas Production Operator" role was successfully completed. The curriculum combined theoretical modules, interactive sessions at the training facility, and direct field observations. The core focus areas included:
Occupational Health and Safety: Reviewing safety protocols for high-risk, hazardous facilities, proper PPE utilization, and emergency response procedures.
Well Construction and Engineering: Understanding drilling mechanics, well trajectories, and structural components (casing strings, wellheads, and bottomhole assemblies).
Production and Exploitation Methods: Analyzing the mechanics of naturally flowing (gushing) wells, as well as artificial lift technologies, specifically Sucker Rod Pumps (SRP) and Electrical Submersible Pumps (ESP).
Maintenance and Overhaul: Studying oil and gas gathering and transportation systems, surface and subsurface equipment components, and the principles of routine well workovers.The internship effectively bridged the gap between first-year academic theory at SIUT and real-world industrial applications. We thoroughly evaluated the structural mechanics of Christmas trees (wellhead structures), pump assemblies, and field automation systems in Karshi. To conclude the program, a comprehensive qualification assessment and final testing were conducted at the training ground, confirming the successful mastery of the primary production operator skill set.

internshipOverview.internshipRole:
Internship Report

During my internship at the Samarkand Metallurgical Plant (SMZ), I became familiar with the work of the accounting department, the foreign economic activity department, and the human resources department. Under the guidance of the Chief Accountant, Mr. Abduvali Daniyarov, I studied the processes of preparing declarations, accounting, and financial reporting in the 1C accounting system, including the use of Account 2910. During the internship, I worked with 1C, E-Contract, Didox.uz, Cargo Customs, and Accounting software, which allowed me to gain practical experience in electronic document management and accounting.

I studied the procedures for export and import operations. On average, the plant exports 40–50 trucks of metal products and imports 5–10 trucks of raw materials and equipment. Export documentation includes a sales contract, a commercial invoice, a TIR Carnet, a Certificate of Origin, and other required documents. The Certificate of Origin may reduce or eliminate customs duties, for example when exporting products from Uzbekistan to the Russian Federation.

Under the supervision of Shokhrukh Aka, I learned how to prepare delivery notes. These documents contain information about the cargo, including the product name, number of coils, total weight, price, exchange rate, place of departure, and destination. For example, one shipment may consist of 4 steel coils with a total weight of 25 tons, while each coil has its own dimensions, weight, and price. I also learned that every product must have its own HS Code (TN VED). Different products such as reinforcing bars, steel profiles, sandwich panels, and steel coils have different HS codes, and using incorrect or non-existent codes is not allowed.

I became familiar with the electronic customs declaration process. After all documents are completed, the customs declaration is submitted online and reviewed by customs officers. Once the declaration is approved, it is downloaded, given to the driver, and the cargo is allowed to leave. I also learned about the responsibilities of customs declarants and the preparation of transport documents, including information about the vehicle's axles.

In addition, I studied the company's recruitment process. It begins with a request from the department manager, specifying the qualifications required for the position, such as knowledge of 1C and Microsoft Excel. After approval, the vacancy is published on hh.uz, where recruiters use artificial intelligence tools to search for suitable candidates. I also learned the importance of preparing a professional CV, as a well-written resume significantly increases employment opportunities.

Final Report

During my internship at the Samarkand Metallurgical Plant (SMZ), I gained valuable practical experience in accounting, export documentation, customs procedures, and business administration. This internship gave me the opportunity to apply the theoretical knowledge I had acquired at Samarkand International University of Technology in a real business environment. It also helped me understand how different departments work together to support the company's production, accounting, logistics, and international trade activities.

Throughout the internship, I worked mainly with the accounting and foreign trade departments. I became familiar with accounting records, declarations, financial reporting, and document management. Under the guidance of experienced employees, I learned how accounting information is processed in the 1C accounting system and how electronic documents are managed through E-Contract, Didox.uz, and Cargo Customs. I also improved my Microsoft Excel skills and learned to use keyboard shortcuts to increase my productivity while working with business documents.

One of my main responsibilities was assisting with the preparation and verification of commercial and logistics documentation. I worked with delivery notes, invoices, contracts, customs declarations, packing documents, and other export-related paperwork. I carefully checked product descriptions, quantities, prices, weights, dimensions, and shipment information before the documents were finalized. I also learned how to prepare documentation for products such as steel coils, galvanized steel, sandwich panels, steel profiles, and reinforcing bars. For example, I learned how shipment documents describe metal coils, including the number of coils, total weight, dimensions, individual weight, and commercial value.

Another important part of my internship was learning about customs procedures and international trade. I became familiar with documents such as the TIR Carnet, commercial invoices, certificates of origin, customs declarations, and transport documents. I learned that every exported product must have the correct HS (TN VED) code and understood why accurate customs classification is essential. I also observed how electronic customs declarations are submitted online and reviewed by customs officers before goods are approved for export.

In addition, I learned about the recruitment process within the company. I observed how new employees are selected, including preparing job requirements, reviewing CVs, using recruitment platforms, and evaluating candidates based on their knowledge of programs such as 1C and Microsoft Excel. This experience helped me understand the importance of professional skills and a well-prepared resume.

During the internship, I developed important professional qualities such as responsibility, attention to detail, teamwork, communication, problem-solving, and time management. Although I initially faced some challenges while adapting to the company's workflow and learning new procedures, I successfully overcame them with practice and guidance from experienced colleagues. These experiences increased my confidence and improved my ability to work in a professional environment.

Overall, this internship was an excellent opportunity to gain practical knowledge and professional experience. It strengthened my understanding of accounting, logistics, customs procedures, and international trade while improving my technical and communication skills. The internship confirmed my interest in building a future career in accounting, finance, logistics, or international business, and it provided me with valuable experience that will support my future professional development.
feedbackForCompany.finalComments: Overall, my internship was a valuable learning experience that helped me develop practical skills in accounting, export documentation, and customs procedures. I appreciate the employees who shared their knowledge and supported my learning. However, I believe the company could improve communication with interns and ensure that internship documents, including signatures and official stamps, are completed on time. Despite these challenges, the internship helped me gain confidence, improve my professional skills, and better prepare for my future career.

internshipOverview.internshipRole: Within the framework of the educational and industrial practicum for the "Management Information System" (MIS) course, I served as an analyst-intern. My task was to study real business processes and IT infrastructure at major Uzbek facilities (the Coca-Cola plant, Samarkand Airport, and the Samarkand Railway Station), as well as to develop a conceptual plan for implementing information systems for the international giant Amazon within the local market.
internshipOverview.keyProjectsTasks:
1. Industrial Excursions: Participated in introductory tours of the Coca-Cola factory, Samarkand Airport, and the Samarkand Railway Station. At these locations, we studied how core business processes work and how digital technologies are used to manage them.
2. MIS Online Course Using Amazon as a Case Study: Studied the theoretical foundations related to organizing, analyzing, and managing large corporations.
3. Group Capstone Project: Prepared a comprehensive strategy for the digital adaptation of Amazon's business in Uzbekistan. Designed a hybrid cloud architecture, proposed IS types (TPS, MIS, DSS, ESS), and outlined corporate system modules (ERP, CRM, SCM).
internshipOverview.skillsDeveloped: The internship program developed both technical and professional skills. I mastered the skills of systematic business process analysis and learned to work with Excel at an advanced level (creating a TPS simulation and a DSS model with dynamic pricing logic). Furthermore, I developed strategic thinking: I learned to correlate the local market characteristics of Uzbekistan (data storage laws, low Visa/Mastercard penetration) with global IS standards.
internshipOverview.challengesFaced: The main challenge was bridging the abstract MIS theory with its practical application in real life. For example, during the excursions, it was hard to immediately see where an ERP system was "hidden" inside the factory or the airport. In the Amazon online project, the main challenge was adapting a global business model to a local market with 90% Cash-on-Delivery payments and strict personal data regulations. I overcame this by combining my observations from the excursions with the theoretical knowledge gained during the online lectures.
internshipOverview.achievements: My main achievement was the successful defense of a comprehensive IS plan for Amazon Uzbekistan in front of the faculty panel. I also gained valuable practical "first-hand" experience by learning during the excursions how the digital economy and logistics actually function at active enterprises in Uzbekistan, and what role modern Information Systems play in this.

reflectionOnLearning.alignmentWithAcademicKnowledge: The academic discipline "Management Information System" (MIS) fully prepared me for this practicum. The theoretical knowledge gained in lectures about Transaction Processing Systems (TPS), Decision Support Systems (DSS), and corporate system architecture (ERP) formed the foundation of my understanding of how the airport and factory operate. The final Amazon case study perfectly demonstrated how MIS theory translates into a tool for real-world business.
reflectionOnLearning.newKnowledgeGained:
1. Local Business Practices in Uzbekistan: I learned how Samarkand Airport generates revenue, how the internal ERP system at the railway station functions, and how production is organized at the Coca-Cola plant.
2. Specifies of the Digital Economy: I realized the critical importance of adapting international standards to local realities—from payment systems like Uzcard/Humo to the legal requirements for server localization.
3. Business Risk Analysis: I learned not only the strengths of IS but also their vulnerabilities (for example, the 2021 AWS outage, which we discussed during the course).
reflectionOnLearning.careerGoals: This internship has solidified my desire to link my career with digital technologies and the development of the Digital Economy sector in Uzbekistan. I realized that I am interested not just in coding, but in seeing the bigger picture—how IT systems manage an entire enterprise. In the future, I would like to become a specialist in implementing and supporting corporate information systems.

feedbackForCompany.companySupport: We were received very warmly at the enterprises (factory, airport, railway station). Employees and managers explained the intricacies of their organizations' operations in detail and were happy to answer all our questions. During the MIS online preparation phase, the university professors provided full methodological support, guiding us through the creation of the final Amazon project.
feedbackForCompany.workEnvironment: The atmosphere at the real enterprises we visited was one of high responsibility and collaborative teamwork, where every employee understands how their work impacts the overall business. The online learning environment was friendly and encouraged active discussion; we felt not just like students, but like a genuine team of MIS consultants.
feedbackForCompany.suggestionsForCompany: As a suggestion for the visited enterprises (particularly the railway station and airport), I would recommend enhancing the digitalization of the customer experience. For example, implementing deeper integration with Telegram (which is highly popular in Uzbekistan) for real-time flight or train status tracking, or implementing elements of a DSS to forecast passenger flow based on holidays (Navruz, Ramadan).
feedbackForCompany.universityPreparation: The university prepared us excellently for the practicum. The structure of the MIS course itself was perfectly designed: first, we mastered the fundamental concepts (TPS, MIS, DSS, ESS), then applied them in practice using Excel (simulations), studied Odoo modules (an ERP analog), and finalized everything with a large-scale Capstone project on opening Amazon in Uzbekistan. The excursions were a fantastic practical supplement to this theoretical foundation.
feedbackForCompany.internshipCoordination: The coordination between the university and the enterprises was organized at a high level. The excursions were planned clearly day-by-day, with no overlaps. The transition from the real-life excursions (offline) to the deep MIS online course was smooth and logical, for which special thanks go to the organizers.
feedbackForCompany.suggestionsForUniversity: The university already provides an excellent knowledge base. To further strengthen the program, I would suggest holding more integrated practical workshops where, right during the excursions (e.g., at the airport), students could not just listen, but try to model a small part of the airport's Transaction Processing System (TPS) on tablets/laptops right on the spot. This would connect MIS theory with real practice immediately.
feedbackForCompany.finalReport:
This internship offered a uniquely balanced experience, combining immersive physical excursions into Uzbekistan's industrial infrastructure with an intensive academic deep-dive into Management Information Systems (MIS) using Amazon as a global benchmark.

The first phase of the internship took us offline, where we visited the Coca-Cola bottling plant, Samarkand International Airport, and the Samarkand Railway Station. As passive observers, we listened to managers explain their daily operational workflows. These visits provided a crucial "ground-level" perspective, showing me how local entities leverage digital systems for logistical coordination, financial tracking, and revenue generation. Seeing the physical side of these operations gave me a concrete framework for the abstract concepts we would later explore.

The second, more academically rigorous phase focused entirely on MIS theory, applied through the lens of Amazon. We explored the fundamental types of Information Systems—TPS, MIS, DSS, and ESS—and learned how they interconnect to run a global corporation. Practically, we built a Transaction Processing System (TPS) simulation in Excel, analyzed Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) modules using the Odoo platform, and created a Decision Support System (DSS) for dynamic pricing. This hands-on practice was invaluable for understanding how data transforms into actionable business intelligence.

The pinnacle of the internship was the Capstone project, where my group acted as MIS consultants. We formulated a complete IS expansion plan for Amazon entering Uzbekistan. To address the local market, our proposal featured a hybrid cloud architecture to comply with strict data sovereignty laws, the integration of local payment rails (Uzcard and Humo) alongside a mandatory Cash-on-Delivery option, and a mobile-first design optimized for 3G connections and Telegram integration, catering to the country's 36+ million smartphone users.

In conclusion, this internship perfectly merged the academic theory of my "Management Information System" (MIS) course at Samarkand International University of Technology with real-world business complexities. It equipped me with a strategic understanding of the Digital Economy and how global standards must be adapted to Central Asian realities. This experience has solidified my ambition to pursue a career in strategic IS management and digital transformation.
feedbackForCompany.finalComments: No comments.

During my internship in the Safety and Fleet department at the American logistics company, I gained invaluable hands-on experience in the core operations of the US trucking industry. My primary responsibility was to assist the safety team in ensuring that the company’s fleet and drivers operated in strict compliance with federal transportation laws and corporate safety standards.

I regularly analyzed Hours of Service (HOS) data to detect and prevent potential violations of Department of Transportation (DOT) and Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) regulations. Whenever discrepancies or potential violations arose, I assisted in communicating with the drivers and dispatchers to resolve the issues promptly and keep operations running smoothly.

In addition to monitoring compliance, I was actively involved in fleet maintenance and safety management. I helped audit driver vehicle inspection reports (DVIR) and tracked vehicle maintenance schedules to ensure the entire fleet remained in safe operating condition. This task required high attention to detail and precise data entry into the company’s fleet management software. I also participated in organizing and reviewing safety documentation for new driver onboarding, ensuring that all background checks, drug test results, and medical certificates met regulatory standards before drivers were dispatched.

A key project I contributed to was a comprehensive internal audit of the fleet’s safety records. Working alongside my mentor, I reviewed historical compliance data to identify recurring safety trends or risk areas. Our findings helped the department update its internal safety brief for drivers, focusing on proactive risk reduction on the road.

In conclusion, this internship allowed me to successfully bridge the gap between my academic knowledge and real-world logistics. It provided me with a deep understanding of safety culture, US transportation regulations, and fleet operations management, which will undoubtedly serve as a solid foundation for my future career in international supply chain logistics.

Our next visit was to Samarkand Railway Station, where I explored its history, passenger services, and operational activities. I learned that the station generates revenue not only through ticket sales but also from cargo transportation and transit services. This visit broadened my understanding of transportation management, logistics, and the role of railway infrastructure in supporting economic development.

I also visited the Samarkand Regional Territorial Department of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Uzbekistan. During this visit, I learned how the organization supports entrepreneurs by providing business consultations, promoting startup development, encouraging exports, and helping companies expand into international markets. This experience strengthened my understanding of entrepreneurship, business development, and the importance of institutional support for economic growth.

The final visit was to Samarkand International Airport, where I became familiar with the airport’s organizational structure and the responsibilities of its various departments. I learned about passenger service operations, airport revenue management, and the roles of the Accounting, Finance, and Economics departments. This visit provided valuable insight into financial management and administrative processes within the aviation industry.

Throughout the internship, I enhanced my communication, analytical, observation, and critical thinking skills by interacting with professionals and observing real business environments. The experience enabled me to apply theoretical concepts learned at university to practical situations and significantly expanded my understanding of business management, finance, logistics, and organizational operations. Overall, the internship was an enriching and rewarding experience that strengthened my professional competencies, increased my confidence, and reinforced my motivation to pursue a successful career in the business field.

As part of my educational experience, I visited the Coca-Cola factory in Samarkand. The visit gave me a valuable opportunity to learn about the production process, quality control, and daily operations of one of the world’s leading beverage companies.

When I arrived at the factory, I was welcomed by the staff and received a short introduction about the history of Coca-Cola and the company’s activities in Uzbekistan. After a safety briefing, I was taken on a guided tour of the production area.

During the tour, I observed how Coca-Cola products are manufactured from start to finish. I saw the modern machines used for washing bottles, filling them with beverages, sealing the caps, and attaching labels. I also watched how the products were packed into boxes and prepared for transportation. The production line was highly automated, and everything was organized efficiently.

I learned about the importance of hygiene and quality control. The factory employees explained how they regularly inspect the products and test the quality of the water, ingredients, and packaging materials. They also described the strict international standards followed to ensure that every bottle is safe for consumers.

In addition, I had the opportunity to ask questions about the manufacturing process, employee responsibilities, and environmental protection. I learned that the factory recycles materials whenever possible and works to reduce water and energy consumption.

Overall, my visit to the Coca-Cola factory in Samarkand was both interesting and educational. It helped me understand how a large manufacturing company operates and how modern technology is used to produce high-quality beverages. This experience increased my knowledge of industrial production and inspired me to learn more about business and manufacturing in the future.

During my intensive internship at Silk Road Destinations, a premier Destination Management Company (DMC), I had the unique opportunity to immerse myself in the highly specialized world of B2B tourism marketing and international partner outreach. Under the direct supervision of the company’s CEO, Ravshan Turakulov, my primary focus was evaluating the efficiency of communication channels, auditing B2B platform engagement, and exploring advanced digital tools to enhance the brand's global footprint.

The core operational philosophy of Silk Road Destinations heavily prioritizes an experiential travel model—focusing on authentic, local, and immersive encounters over traditional sightseeing. My role involved aligning marketing narratives with this philosophy, ensuring that outreach materials effectively communicated the value of artisan workshops, local market experiences, and high-end MICE capabilities to international agents. Despite the highly compressed timeframe of this internship, it served as a powerful catalyst for practical learning. I actively analyzed workflows for platforms like EVINTRA and worked on optimizing B2B messaging templates to ensure they met strict professional communication standards.

A significant takeaway from this experience was the practical integration of cutting-edge AI tools into modern tourism workflows. Navigating the balance between rapid digital content creation and authentic brand voice was both a challenge and a major skill acquired. This experience successfully bridged the gap between my academic marketing knowledge and real-world application, proving that impactful strategy relies on a deep understanding of niche market dynamics.

Ultimately, this brief but dense experience provided invaluable insights into the business-to-business travel ecosystem. It reinforced my career aspirations to spearhead digital marketing strategies within international tourism, demonstrating how modern technological adoption can elevate traditional destination management. Moving forward, I highly recommend that the university continues fostering partnerships with forward-thinking DMCs like Silk Road Destinations to give students a realistic look into the future of global tourism.
And yeah, one more thing, I officially work here.

I analyzed recent digital reviews and suggested a more proactive verbal check-in questionnaire to capture guest dissatisfaction before departure. In conclusion, this internship provided me with invaluable practical experience. The experience confirmed my career aspiration to advance in business administration and operations management. It strengthened my analytical thinking, expanded my professional network, and gave me practical insights that will support my future career. The internship was an excellent opportunity to observe real business environments and better understand how different industries operate successfully.

During my internship, I visited several organizations related to my field of study, including CCI, Samarkand International Airport, Samarkand Railway Station, and the Samarkand Regional Territorial Department of the Chamber of Commerce. As a first-year student, my role was mainly to observe how these organizations operate, listen to presentations, ask questions, and take notes throughout each visit. 
At CCI, we were taken on a journey of the history of the company and how it has evolved over the years to become one of the leading beverage producers in the region. According to the representatives, CCI operates in a number of countries and continues to expand its production facilities in Uzbekistan, which shows the company’s long-term commitment to the economic development of the country. We also learned how the company operates on a day-to-day basis, how new equipment is inspected and tested before it goes into service, and how the various departments communicate with each other to ensure an efficient production process. It was particularly interesting to see how Management Information Systems (MIS) assist with communication, data management, and decision-making throughout the organization. 
The visit to Samarkand International Airport was the most memorable for me. We learned about the airport's financial structure, how it generates revenue, and how the finance, accounting, and economics departments work together. I was especially interested in learning about budgeting, forecasting, and how financial decisions are made to ensure the airport continues to operate efficiently. It was also fascinating to see how digital technologies play an important role in improving communication, coordination, and overall efficiency across different departments.
We also became familiar with the structure of the station and the services of the Samarkand Railway Station: ticket office, VIP lounge, sleeping capsules and other passenger services. We also got to know that the station has around 5,500-6,000 passengers per day and generates revenue through ticket sales, loading and unloading and transit services. This visit helped me understand better the importance of the customer service and effective management of transportation organizations. 
During our visit to the Samarkand Regional Territorial Department of the Chamber of Commerce, we learned about the organization’s role in supporting local businesses, entrepreneurs, and investment activities in the region. The visit helped me better understand how business support institutions contribute to economic development and cooperation between companies.
Overall, the internship gave me valuable experience that helped me connect the theoretical knowledge from my Digital Economy studies with practical examples from industry.

During my internship at MTP Siyob Agromash LLC, I worked as a Foreign Economic Activity (FEA) specialist, focusing on import procurement, supplier relations, and inventory management for tire and automotive parts imported from China, Russia, and CIS countries.
One of my main responsibilities was HS code classification for various automotive parts, including wheel discs, brake components, and tire assemblies. This required careful attention to detail, as similar-looking parts often fall under different customs codes depending on their function and specifications. I learned to distinguish between items such as wheel discs and brake rotors, and to correctly classify disk-and-tire assemblies for customs clearance.
Another significant part of my work involved handling supplier warranty claims (reklamatsiya) for defective products. I drafted and managed correspondence with factories in China and Russia regarding issues such as defective inner tubes, tread separation, and stone drilling damage on tires used in quarry environments. This process taught me how to build a claim with strong supporting evidence, including photos, mileage data, and clear technical explanations, and how to negotiate fair resolutions when initial claims were rejected on technical grounds.
I also worked extensively with the company's 1C accounting system, performing inventory reconciliation by comparing physical stock counts with system records to identify discrepancies and surpluses or shortages. Additionally, I built and maintained Excel-based sales tracking tools for different tire brands, using formulas such as SUMIF and VLOOKUP to organize data by product type, size, and year for better business analysis.
Throughout the internship, I improved my professional communication skills, writing business correspondence in English and Russian tailored to different international suppliers. I also strengthened my Excel skills significantly, moving from basic formulas to more advanced data organization techniques.
This internship gave me practical, real-world experience that complemented my academic studies and confirmed my interest in pursuing a career in foreign trade and international business. I gained a much deeper understanding of the complexities involved in import operations, from customs classification to supplier negotiations, and I plan to continue building expertise in this field.

internshipOverview.challengesFaced:
Detached ORM instances in background tasks — FastAPI's BackgroundTasks executed after the DB session was closed, causing DetachedInstanceError
Corporate LDAP/AD integration — Configuring ldap3 to authenticate against Microsoft Active Directory with sAMAccountName format and fallback to local bcrypt for admin accounts
Telegram Bot token not propagated — The TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN was defined in .env but not passed to the app container in Docker Compose, causing silent failures in notification delivery
internshipOverview.achievements:
Delivered a fully production-ready Safety Management System from scratch
Replaced a commercial SMS platform (SMS Pro: $3,000 setup + $3,300/month) with an in-house solution, saving $42,600+ in the first year
Passed load testing at 200+ concurrent users with 0% error rate across all endpoints

reflectionOnLearning.alignmentWithAcademicKnowledge:
My coursework provided a strong theoretical foundation that proved directly applicable throughout the internship.
Database Management Systems (DBMS) gave me a solid understanding of relational data modelling, SQL, transactions, and constraints — essential for designing the PostgreSQL schema with 16 tables, foreign keys, and the migration of all datetime columns to timezone-aware types (timestamptz).
Network Programming introduced me to client-server architecture, HTTP, and socket communication, which directly underpinned working with REST APIs (FastAPI), Docker networking between containers, and integrating external services such as Telegram Bot API and LDAP/Active Directory over TCP.
Operating Systems provided the foundation for working confidently on Ubuntu Server — managing processes, file systems, cron jobs for automated backups, and understanding how Docker isolates containers at the OS level.
Automata Theory, while the most abstract of the four, reinforced structured thinking around state machines — a concept that translated well into designing the ConversationHandler flow in the Telegram Bot (registration states: language selection -> username input -> pending approval).
Overall, the academic curriculum ensured I could move from theory to implementation without needing to build foundational knowledge from scratch during the internship.
reflectionOnLearning.newKnowledgeGained:
Full-Stack Web Development — Building a complete production application with FastAPI (async Python backend) and React (component-based frontend with i18n, state management, and responsive design) was entirely self-taught during the internship.
Containerization with Docker — While OS coursework covered processes and isolation concepts, practical Docker and Docker Compose usage — multi-container orchestration, networking between services, volume management, and production deployment — was new territory.
Authentication & Security Patterns — Implementing JWT-based authentication, OAuth2 password flow, bcrypt password hashing, and LDAP/Active Directory integration were not part of the academic syllabus.
reflectionOnLearning.careerGoals:
Before the internship, my career direction was broadly defined as "software development" — without a clear sense of specialisation or industry. This experience brought significant clarity.
Confirmed interest in backend and systems development. Designing and deploying a full production system — from database schema to API to deployment infrastructure — showed me that backend engineering and system architecture is where I genuinely enjoy working. Seeing the system go live and be used by real people in an operational environment was a strong motivator.
Introduced me to the intersection of software and safety-critical domains. Working within aviation ground handling exposed me to how software directly supports regulatory compliance (ICAO, ISAGO) and operational safety. This is a niche I had not previously considered, but one I find meaningful — software that has a real impact on safety outcomes is more compelling to me than general-purpose applications.
Shifted my perspective from academic to production thinking. University projects have a defined scope and a deadline after which they disappear. This internship taught me what it means to build something that has to keep running — backups, monitoring, error handling, multi-user access control, and backward-compatible changes. That mindset shift feels permanent.
Strengthened my goal of becoming a well-rounded engineer. Having touched backend, frontend, DevOps, database design, and bot development within a single project, I now have a clearer picture of what a full-stack engineer actually does — and a stronger motivation to deepen expertise across all of these areas.

feedbackForCompany.companySupport:

Room for growth. The organisation expressed openness to expanding the system further — additional integrations, broader deployment, and continued development — which signals long-term investment in both the project and the people behind it.
Overall, the environment was more enabling than prescriptive, which suited the nature of the project and accelerated both technical and professional development.
feedbackForCompany.workEnvironment:
The work environment at Air Marakanda reflected the nature of aviation operations — structured, safety-conscious, and process-oriented, while remaining approachable at the team level.
Safety-first culture. Unsurprisingly for an aviation company, safety permeates every aspect of operations. Procedures, reporting, and accountability are not bureaucratic formalities but genuinely held values. Working within this environment made the purpose of the SMS project feel concrete rather than abstract — every feature built had a real operational counterpart.
Multilingual and multicultural workplace. Day-to-day communication naturally flowed across Russian, Uzbek, and English depending on the context and the audience. This directly shaped product decisions — the trilingual support built into both the web application and the Telegram Bot was not a technical exercise but a genuine organisational necessity.
Operational pace. Ground handling is a 24/7 operation tied to flight schedules, which means the surrounding environment is always active. This created a healthy sense of urgency — features were not developed speculatively but in response to real, immediate needs expressed by the team.
Collaborative access without micromanagement. Colleagues from different departments — operations, compliance, IT — were accessible for questions and feedback throughout the project. Input from end users shaped several design decisions, from department naming conventions to notification preferences.
Professional growth encouraged. The organisation demonstrated willingness to invest in internal tooling and homegrown solutions rather than defaulting to off-the-shelf products, which reflects a culture that values technical initiative and trusts its people to deliver.
feedbackForCompany.suggestionsForCompany: Introduce a dedicated server for the production environment. Currently the system runs on a shared internal server. As the user base grows and the system becomes more operationally critical, migrating to a dedicated machine with external NAS-based backup storage would significantly improve reliability and disaster recovery capability.
feedbackForCompany.universityPreparation:
The academic programme at Samarkand International University of Technology provided a solid theoretical foundation that proved genuinely useful during the internship. Core subjects such as DBMS, Network Programming, Operating Systems, and Automata Theory each had direct practical applications — from database schema design to server administration to understanding client-server communication. The theoretical grounding meant that encountering new tools and frameworks during the internship required learning syntax and conventions, not entirely new concepts.
Areas Where the University Could Improve
That said, the gap between academic knowledge and production readiness was notable in several areas:
Practical web development. The curriculum does not appear to cover modern full-stack development — REST API design, frontend frameworks, or deployment pipelines. These skills were entirely self-taught during the internship and represent the largest gap between what was studied and what was needed on day one.
Containerisation and DevOps basics. Docker, Nginx configuration, and Linux server administration in a production context are increasingly fundamental skills that are absent from the current curriculum.
Suggestion for the university: Introducing even one applied course covering REST API development, Docker basics would significantly reduce the learning curve for students entering technical internships and make graduates more immediately effective in industry roles.
feedbackForCompany.internshipCoordination:
University coordination with the company was present in its formal aspects — the internship placement was arranged through established channels, and the necessary documentation and reporting requirements were clearly communicated from the outset.
In practice, however, the day-to-day internship experience was largely independent of university involvement. The work was driven by the company's operational needs and the intern's own initiative rather than by academic oversight or structured coordination between the two institutions.
feedbackForCompany.suggestionsForUniversity:
Before the internship:
The university could introduce a brief pre-internship preparation module covering practical skills that consistently appear in technical placements — Git and version control workflows, REST API fundamentals, Linux command line basics, and Docker. Even a condensed two-week course would meaningfully reduce the initial adjustment period for students entering technical roles.
During the internship:
A structured midpoint check-in — involving the student, a university supervisor, and ideally a company representative — would provide an opportunity to address challenges early, ensure the experience remains educationally relevant, and demonstrate to host companies that the university is an active partner rather than a passive certifying body.
feedbackForCompany.finalReport:
Internship Report — Air Marakanda, Samarkand International Airport
During my internship at Air Marakanda, I worked as a Software Developer within the IT department, with the primary objective of designing and delivering a fully functional Safety Management System (SMS) tailored to the operational needs of the ground handling division at Samarkand International Airport.
Primary Project: SMS Web Application
The central project was the end-to-end development of SMS — a production-grade web platform built on FastAPI (Python) for the backend, React for the frontend, and PostgreSQL as the database. The system was deployed on a corporate Ubuntu 24.04 server using Docker Compose, with Nginx handling HTTPS termination.
My responsibilities covered the full development lifecycle. On the backend, I designed a normalised relational schema across 16 tables, implemented 14 API routers covering incident logging (Safety Log), bulletin management, SPI indicator tracking, risk assessment, hazard library, user management, and audit logging. I integrated Microsoft Active Directory via LDAP for single sign-on authentication supporting 325 corporate users, with a bcrypt fallback for local accounts.
On the frontend, I built ten React pages with full trilingual support (Russian, English, Uzbek) using react-i18next, a responsive collapsible sidebar, and data visualisations using Recharts. The application included an Excel export module generating ISAGO-compliant compliance reports across four structured sheets.
Notification System
I implemented a four-channel notification system: in-app notifications, Web Push (VAPID), email via corporate SMTP, and a Telegram Bot. The Telegram Bot was built using python-telegram-bot 21.6 with multilingual support, a reply keyboard navigation menu, and inline acknowledgement buttons that allowed users to confirm bulletin receipt directly within Telegram. Email and Telegram delivery were refactored into FastAPI BackgroundTasks to eliminate response latency.
Infrastructure and Operations
I configured automated backup scripts running on cron — hourly database dumps and daily full backups with a two-week retention policy — and built a web-based backup management UI accessible to administrators. Load testing with Locust confirmed the system handles 200+ concurrent users with a 0% error rate across all endpoints.
The system was delivered fully operational and is currently in active use across seven departments of Air Marakanda.
feedbackForCompany.finalComments: This internship was, without question, the most formative technical experience of my academic journey so far. What made it distinct from university projects was not the complexity of the technologies involved, but the weight of real consequence — the system had to work reliably, be understood by non-technical users across three languages, and remain maintainable beyond the internship period.

feedbackForCompany.finalReport:
As a logistics expeditor, I was responsible for ensuring shipments moved through the delivery process without delay. While dispatchers handled the initial planning and scheduling of freight, I stepped in once a shipment was already in motion — actively monitoring, troubleshooting, and intervening whenever something threatened to slow it down.

My core responsibility was proactive problem-solving. I tracked shipments in real time using GPS and transportation management systems (TMS), identified potential delays before they escalated, and coordinated directly with drivers, carriers, warehouses, and customers to resolve issues. I regularly handled problems such as mechanical breakdowns, weather disruptions, border crossing delays, missing documentation, and capacity shortages at receiving docks.

I also served as the primary point of contact between multiple parties — shippers, carriers, brokers, and clients — keeping everyone updated on shipment status, particularly for high-priority or time-sensitive freight. This involved arranging expedited transportation methods, rerouting shipments, and securing last-minute carrier capacity when original plans fell through.

Documentation and compliance were a key part of my role as well. I made sure bills of lading, proof of delivery, customs paperwork, and other required documents were accurate and submitted on time, especially for cross-border or regulated freight like hazmat shipments.

In my experience with just-in-time manufacturing and perishable goods, I understood how critical my role was in preventing costly production stoppages or spoiled inventory. I measured my own success by on-time delivery rates and my ability to minimize disruptions across the supply chain.

Through this role, I combined urgency, adaptability, and strong communication skills to keep the supply chain moving smoothly — acting as the last line of defense against delays that could otherwise ripple through an entire distribution network.

During my internship, I had the opportunity to visit several important organizations in Samarkand and learn how they operate in real life. As a student of the Digital Economy program, this experience was useful for me because it helped me connect my academic knowledge with practical business processes.

Our first visit was to Samarkand Railway Station. We learned about the station’s facilities, passenger services, ticket counters, VIP lounge, and general infrastructure. I found it interesting that the station provides different services for different passenger categories, including travelers who have several train transfers and need a comfortable place to rest.

We also visited a historic venue in Samarkand where PROSNAB Service held business discussions. During this visit, I learned more about the role of business meetings, entrepreneurship, and industrial solutions in the food production sector. The building itself was also impressive because of its preserved Soviet-era ceremonial hall.

Another important visit was to Samarkand International Airport. The staff explained how the airport works behind the scenes, including passenger service, cargo, aircraft handling, parking areas, and the runway. I also learned that a large part of airport income comes from aviation fuel, as well as shops, restaurants, parking, and other services. It was interesting to know that the airport was rebuilt and modernized in 2022.

We also visited a Coca-Cola factory in Uzbekistan. The factory staff showed us how drinks are produced, filled, packaged, and checked for quality. We learned that the company produces Coca-Cola, Fanta, Sprite, Fuse Tea, Bonaqua, Cappy, and other drinks. Seeing modern machines and the production process helped me understand how large-scale manufacturing works.

Overall, this internship was informative and useful. It improved my communication, observation, and report-writing skills. Most importantly, it helped me understand how different industries manage their services, resources, and daily operations. This experience motivated me to continue developing my knowledge and prepare better for my future career.

My internship took place at a tourist center that offers traditional handicraft experiences and introduces visitors to the culture and traditions of our country. During this period, I became involved not only in the daily activities of the company but also in planning and improving its services.

At the beginning of my internship, I observed how the center operated and gradually took on more responsibilities. I participated in preparing handicraft workshops by coordinating schedules with artisans and making sure that all necessary arrangements had been completed before each event. During the workshops, I supervised the overall organization, welcomed visitors, and helped create a comfortable and friendly atmosphere for both guests and craftsmen.

An important part of my work was interacting with tourists and tour guides. I answered visitors’ questions about local traditions and crafts and shared interesting facts about the history and cultural heritage of our country. After each workshop, I discussed the experience with guides and collected their opinions about what visitors enjoyed most and what could be improved in future events. This allowed the team to better understand customer expectations and continuously improve the quality of the activities.

As the internship continued, the tourist season came to an end and the number of international visitors decreased. Instead of simply waiting for the next season, our team started looking for new opportunities to keep the center active. Together with my supervisor and colleagues, I participated in discussions about how to make our workshops more attractive for local residents. We explored different ideas and considered ways to encourage people to reconnect with their own culture through creative and educational experiences.

Working on this initiative helped me understand that successful businesses must constantly adapt to changing circumstances. I saw how teamwork, creativity, and careful planning are used to solve real business challenges. I also gained a better understanding of how customer interests influence business decisions and how new ideas are developed before being introduced.

Overall, this internship allowed me to connect theoretical knowledge with practical experience. It improved my communication and organizational skills, increased my confidence in a professional environment, and gave me a deeper understanding of how a tourism business operates while preserving and promoting national culture.

feedbackForCompany.finalReport:
An internship within the banking system is a unique and high-stakes introduction to the professional world. As an intern, stepping onto the banking floor provides a front-row seat to the financial engine that powers the global economy. However, like any rigorous professional environment, the experience comes with a distinct set of trade-offs. Reflecting on my time in the banking sector reveals a clear ledger of invaluable advantages alongside demanding disadvantages, both of which have fundamentally shaped my professional outlook.
The benefits of a banking internship extend far beyond a prestigious line on a resume. The environment acts as an incubator for rapid professional and personal development.
• Accelerated Skill Acquisition: Banking forces an immediate upgrade in both technical and soft skills. From mastering financial modeling and data analysis to learning the nuances of corporate communication, the learning curve is steep but incredibly rewarding.
While the professional gains are substantial, they come at a cost. The banking sector is notoriously demanding, and the internship highlighted several challenging realities of the industry.
• High Stress and Intense Pressure: The banking environment is fast-paced and high-stakes. The pressure to deliver flawless work under tight deadlines can be mentally taxing, occasionally leading to a stressful and overwhelming daily routine.
 Repetitive and Administrative Tasks As an intern, not every task is high finance or strategic planning. A significant portion of the workload often involves routine administrative duties, repetitive data entry, or tedious compliance paperwork. Navigating this bureaucratic side of banking requires a lot of patience.
Conclusion: Balancing the Investment
Ultimately, my internship in the banking system was a balanced investment in my future. The disadvantages—the long hours, stress, and routine paperwork—were the price of admission to a premier professional arena. The advantages—the sharp analytical mindset, the industry insights, and the resilience I developed—far outweigh the challenges. Whether I choose to pursue a lifelong career in finance or apply these skills to another industry, the ledger of this experience remains firmly in the positive, having transformed me from a student into a grounded professional.
